summary: Recommends what information a site should publish for each service it offers over the ARPANET. There are two kinds: details programmers need to connect to the service, and details a user needs to use it. Together these form a functional document, as described in RFC 115.

eli5.summary: If you open a lemonade stand, you should post a sign saying what you sell, the price, and where to stand. This note says every network service should post the same kind of sign.

questions: what documentation should an arpanet service provide
what documentation should network services provide
how should network services be documented
subtitle: What network services should document for users and programmers

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET services varied widely, and sites had no clear guidance on what information to publish so other sites could use them.
tldr.mechanism: Sites should publish two types of documentation: technical details for programmers (connection sockets, message formats, character sets) and user information (login sequences, command syntax, special behaviors for network users).
tldr.outcome: Clear documentation enables network use of services and reduces support burden. The Network Information Center would distribute and maintain these functional documents.

today: RFC 118 establishes the principle that network services should have clear documentation. This became standard practice as ARPANET services proliferated.

sections.title: Documentation for Network Services
sections.content: Each service available over the ARPANET needs to publish two types of information. First, system programmers at other sites need technical details: the connection socket numbers, message formats, character set information, and protocol details required to establish a connection. Second, users at other sites need to know how to actually use the service: login sequences, command syntax, and how the service behaves differently for network users versus local users.
sections.eli5: A network service is like a restaurant. Programmers need the address and phone number. Users need to know the menu and hours.

sections.title: User Information Requirements
sections.content:
User information should address three categories: information unique to network users (e.g., different login procedures), information shared between network and local users, and local site customizations for network use. Initially, sites would adapt their existing local user manuals by adding a supplement for network users covering differences in echo behavior, character handling, and available features.

Even when there are no differences between network and local use, this should be explicitly stated to avoid confusion.
sections.eli5: Tell network users what is the same as local use and what is different. If everything is the same, say so clearly.

sections.title: Distribution and Management
sections.content: The Network Information Center would distribute and maintain one copy of each functional document at each Network Station. Sites would submit 100 copies of their documentation to the NIC, which would make them available in the NIC Collection. Users could obtain copies directly from the service site or from their local NIC Collection. Each documentation package should include contact information and pricing for additional copies.
sections.eli5: One central library (the NIC) would keep a copy of every service manual. Sites send their documentation there, and users can copy it from the library.
